blocks.text: A **lymphoma** is a malignant tumour of lymphoid cells that live mainly in lymphoid tissue (nodes, spleen, mucosal lymphoid tissue). The diagnosis is made on **biopsy histology**, which splits lymphomas into **Hodgkin lymphoma (HL)** and **non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL)**. Most lymphomas of both kinds are of **B-cell** origin. NHL is a **monoclonal** proliferation, and Davidson puts it at about **90% B-cell and 10% T-cell**.

blocks.title: Grade: how fast the tumour divides (mainly an NHL concept)
items: **High grade:** rapid proliferation, history of **weeks**, frequent **extranodal** disease. It can be life-threatening and is fatal if untreated, but it is **potentially curable**.
**Low grade:** slow proliferation, often present for **months** before diagnosis, with an **indolent** course. It is **not curable** with conventional therapy.

blocks.title: HL vs NHL: epidemiology (Davidson figures)
rows: Median 31 y; **bimodal**, peaks at 20–35 and 50–70 y
Median 65–70 y; incidence climbs with age (rare before 40)
DLBCL (~30%) then follicular (~20%): together > two-thirds of NHL

blocks.text: Taken together, lymphomas run at about **15–20 per 100 000** a year, making them the **fifth commonest malignancy** in the West and more frequent than leukaemia. Roughly **20%** start at a **primary extranodal site** rather than in a node.

blocks.title: Aetiology of Hodgkin lymphoma
items: The cause is **unknown**. HL is commoner in people from well-educated backgrounds and small families.

A past history of **infectious mononucleosis** triples the risk, but a causal role for **EBV** is not proven. Up to 40% of patients have raised EBV antibody titres at diagnosis, and EBV DNA has been found in HL tissue.
Quick sources also list **HIV**, autoimmune disease (e.g. RA, sarcoidosis) and family history.

blocks.title: NHL: infections and conditions linked to specific lymphomas
rows: NHL is a late, **AIDS-defining** complication (relative risk ~60–100×)

blocks.text: Endemic Burkitt lymphoma is **always EBV-associated** and follows the **malaria belt** of equatorial Africa. Exam pairing: Burkitt with EBV, malaria and HIV.
Sources disagree on the **B : T split** in NHL: Davidson gives **90 : 10**, Kumar & Clark and the Essentials ~80 : 20, and Pocket Medicine/Step-Up ~85 : 15. Davidson's 90% is the figure to quote.

HL epidemiology numbers vary too. Kumar quotes **~3/100 000** with M : F 1.3 : 1 and a third-decade peak, and quick sources give age peaks of ~20 and ~75 years. Learn Davidson's figures: **~4/100 000, 1.5 : 1, peaks 20–35 and 50–70 years**.

B cells are selected for antigen in the **germinal (follicle) centre** of the node. Mistakes during this process produce **B-cell lymphomas**, which are by far the most common type. More generally, NHL is a **clonal expansion** frozen at a particular stage of lymphocyte development. Malignant change usually comes from errors in **class switching** or in **immunoglobulin / T-cell receptor gene recombination**, so the breakpoints often lie in Ig or TCR loci. Tumours of **mature, non-dividing** cells are **indolent**, while those of **proliferating** cells (lymphoblasts, immunoblasts) are **aggressive**.

blocks.title: Signature translocations in NHL
rows: **MYC** moved next to IGH: drives proliferation

blocks.text: The hallmark of HL is the **Reed–Sternberg (RS) cell**, a large malignant cell of **B-cell origin**. It has two (or more) nuclei, each with a prominent eosinophilic nucleolus, giving the **"owl's eyes"** look. RS cells make up **< 1%** of the node. The rest is a reactive background of T cells, B cells, plasma cells, eosinophils and fibroblasts, and this inflammatory background helps separate HL from NHL. Classical RS cells are **CD15+, CD30+ and usually CD20−**.

blocks.title: WHO classification of Hodgkin lymphoma
rows: "Popcorn" cells, strongly **CD20+**; behaves like low-grade B-cell NHL (slow, localised, rarely fatal)
Young adults and **women**; collagen bands; **mediastinal** disease; usually stage I–II
Older patients; more often advanced stage
Seen with HIV; worst prognosis; probably large-cell/anaplastic NHL in many cases

blocks.title: Classifying NHL
items: The WHO system sorts NHL by **lineage** (B vs T/NK) and **maturation stage** (precursor vs mature), and adds histology, cytogenetics and clinical features.
At the bedside, **grade** (proliferation rate) matters most. **DLBCL** is the classic high-grade lymphoma and **follicular** the classic low-grade one.
Histology: a **follicular (nodular)** pattern suggests low grade, and a **diffuse** sheet of cells suggests high grade.
**Mantle cell** lymphoma has low-grade-looking histology but behaves aggressively and carries a poor prognosis.
Less common types include Burkitt, mantle cell, MALT and T-cell lymphomas.

blocks.title: Subtypes worth knowing
rows: The **fastest-proliferating** lymphoma. Three forms: **endemic** (always EBV, malaria belt, jaw), **sporadic** (children and young adults, often abdominal) and **immunodeficiency-related** (HIV, post-transplant).
Arises in chronically inflamed mucosa: stomach (_H. pylori_), salivary gland (Sjögren). Usually indolent.
Cutaneous **T-cell** lymphoma: eczema-like patches progressing to erythroderma. Sézary syndrome = skin plus circulating cells.
Rarer than B-cell types and **CD20-negative**. ALK-positive anaplastic large-cell lymphoma does better than other T-cell types.

blocks.note: Look at: the large binucleate Reed–Sternberg cell with prominent eosinophilic nucleoli, sitting among small reactive lymphocytes.
Compare: follicular/nodular pattern (low-grade NHL) vs diffuse effacement of the node (high-grade NHL).

blocks.text: In classical HL the histological subtype changes the prognosis little, except **lymphocyte-depleted** disease, which has the worst outlook.

Step-Up calls **follicular** the commonest NHL and lists "lymphocyte predominance" among four HL subtypes. Follow the WHO/Davidson scheme instead: **DLBCL is the commonest lymphoma** (~30%, follicular second at ~20%), and nodular lymphocyte-predominant HL is the **non-classical** type, separate from classical lymphocyte-rich HL.

blocks.title: Presentation: HL vs NHL
rows: Painless, **rubbery**, usually cervical or supraclavicular; size may fluctuate
Painless, firm, mobile; often at several sites
**Contiguous**, node to next node; isolated below-diaphragm disease < 10%
Common: marrow, gut, thyroid, lung, skin, testis, brain
Young patients with nodular sclerosis: large, often **silent** mass or dry cough and breathlessness
A minority of DLBCL present with a primary mediastinal mass
~35% B symptoms; itch in 10–15%; **alcohol-induced nodal pain**; Pel-Ebstein fever
B symptoms ~15–50% by subtype; sweats, weight loss, fever, itch
Can be involved (that is stage IV); assessed by PET-CT, with marrow biopsy only if PET is not used
Low grade **50–60%**, high grade ~10%, causing anaemia, leukopenia or thrombocytopenia

blocks.title: B symptoms (count for staging)
items: Fever **> 38°C**
Drenching **night sweats**
Unexplained loss of **> 10% body weight** within 6 months

blocks.title: NHL: compression and organ syndromes
items: Gut obstruction and ascites; GI lymphoma can cause early satiety, vomiting and weight loss
**Superior vena cava obstruction**
**Spinal cord compression**
Cytopenias from marrow infiltration; rash in cutaneous lymphoma; hepatosplenomegaly

blocks.title: Subtype clues in the history
rows: Young African child with a **rapidly growing jaw tumour**. Next commonest is an abdominal mass with marrow involvement; CNS, kidney and testis also occur.
Rapidly enlarging painless mass, often in someone over 65; fatal within months if untreated
Older men (M : F 3 : 1), generalised nodes, marrow and blood involvement, multiple bowel lesions
Dyspepsia, ulcer-type symptoms, bleeding or a gastric mass

blocks.note: Look at: a widened mediastinum from a mediastinal nodal mass in Hodgkin lymphoma.
Look at: bulky axillary nodes with distended superficial veins in high-grade lymphoma.
Look at: a child with facial and jaw swelling from Burkitt lymphoma.

blocks.text: **Pain in the nodes after drinking alcohol** and generalised **pruritus** are classic HL clues. Neither is a B symptom, so neither changes the stage.
Hepatosplenomegaly in HL does **not always** mean the liver or spleen is involved. Likewise, abnormal LFTs may occur without hepatic infiltration.

Lymphoma is a **tissue diagnosis**. Take an **excision biopsy** of a node big enough for histology, immunophenotyping and molecular studies. A **core biopsy** (e.g. CT-guided) is acceptable for deep, impalpable disease. **Fine needle aspiration is inadequate** because it loses the nodal architecture. Biopsy any node **> 1 cm** that persists for **> 4 weeks** without an infective cause.

blocks.title: Work-up of a patient with lymphoma
rows: May be normal. In HL, **anaemia or lymphopenia** is a poor prognostic sign, and eosinophilia or neutrophilia may occur. Cytopenias suggest marrow disease.
Often raised in HL and tracks disease activity
May be abnormal with or without liver infiltration; an **obstructive pattern** suggests **porta hepatis nodes**
**Raised LDH is an adverse** prognostic factor
Very high in aggressive NHL, with a risk of renal failure when treatment starts
IgG or IgM paraprotein can act as a response marker
**HIV, hepatitis B (HBsAg + anti-HBc) and C** before rituximab
CXR (mediastinal mass); CT chest/abdomen/pelvis; **FDG-PET-CT** for staging and response
NHL staging; only needed if PET is not used to assess marrow
Defines lineage and subtype; detects translocations and Ig/TCR gene rearrangements

blocks.title: Differential of generalised lymphadenopathy
items: Infection: EBV, CMV, toxoplasma, TB, HIV
Malignancy: lymphoma, leukaemia
Systemic disease: SLE, sarcoidosis, rheumatoid arthritis
Drugs, e.g. phenytoin

blocks.text: **PET** separates an active residual mass (FDG-avid) from **fibrosis or necrosis** (PET-negative) after chemotherapy, which guides whether radiotherapy is needed.

**Tumour lysis:** very aggressive NHL (especially **Burkitt**) can have a very high urate and precipitate renal failure once treatment begins. Give **rasburicase** prophylaxis and check potassium and phosphate very frequently for at least **72 hours**.

blocks.note: Look at: an anterior mediastinal mass pushing the trachea aside on CXR; intense FDG uptake at diagnosis and loss of uptake (complete response) after treatment.
Look at: CT-guided needle biopsy of enlarged retroperitoneal nodes, the route for occult disease.
Look at: circulating mantle cell lymphoma cells that can mimic CLL, so immunophenotyping/cytogenetics is needed.

blocks.title: Ann Arbor staging (Cotswolds modification)
rows: One lymph node region (I), or one extralymphatic site (IE)
≥ 2 node regions on the **same side** of the diaphragm (II), or an extralymphatic site plus nodes on that side (IIE)
Node regions on **both sides** of the diaphragm, ± spleen (IIIS) or localised extralymphatic site (IIIE)
**Diffuse** involvement of extralymphatic tissue, e.g. liver or bone marrow

blocks.title: Stage suffixes
rows: Fever > 38°C, drenching night sweats, or > 10% weight loss in 6 months
**Bulk**: mediastinal widening > 1/3, or a nodal mass > 10 cm
A single extranodal site contiguous with known nodal disease

blocks.text: The same staging system is used for **HL and NHL**, but NHL is much more often **stage III–IV** at presentation. Lymphatic structures include the nodes, **spleen**, thymus, Waldeyer's ring, appendix and Peyer's patches. In NHL, the **histological subtype** shapes treatment and prognosis more than the stage does.

blocks.title: Hodgkin lymphoma prognosis
items: Adverse features: **bulk > 10 cm**, anaemia, lymphopenia, **raised LDH**, B symptoms.
Early-unfavourable criteria (Pocket): age > 50, bulky mediastinum, B symptoms, ESR > 50, > 3 nodal sites.
Early stage: > 90% reach complete remission with chemotherapy plus involved-field RT, and most are cured.
Advanced stage: historically 50–70% cured, now beyond 80% long-term survival with PET-directed therapy.
Primary refractory disease or relapse within a year carries a poor prognosis.

blocks.title: Hasenclever index (advanced HL): 1 point each
rows: Score 0–1: ~90% 5-year overall survival (79% progression-free); highest scores ~59% OS

blocks.title: NHL prognostic indices
rows: Older age (> 60), stage III–IV, > 1 extranodal site, raised LDH, poor performance status (ECOG ≥ 2)
Age > 60, stage III–IV, Hb < 120 g/L, > 4 nodal areas, raised LDH
Guides choice and intensity of therapy

blocks.title: NHL outcome figures
items: Low-grade NHL: relapsing–remitting, median survival ~**12 years**. It transforms to high grade at **~3% per year**, with poor survival after transformation.
DLBCL on R-CHOP: ~75% respond, ~50% disease-free at 5 years. Relapse carries < 10% 5-year survival, and HSCT helps patients under 65.
Activated B-cell (ABC) DLBCL and **MYC + BCL2/BCL6 "double-hit"** rearrangements do worse.
Overall NHL 5-year survival is ~65%.

blocks.text: The Hasenclever survival percentages differ between Davidson and Kumar & Clark. Use **Davidson's** figures (score 0–1 gives ~90% 5-year OS). The **seven factors** are the same in both, and they are the examinable part.

blocks.title: HL treatment by setting (Davidson / UK practice)
rows: Early, with risk factors (bulk, high ESR)
**6–8 cycles ABVD**, with an interim PET after 2 cycles
Drop bleomycin and finish with **AVD** (less lung toxicity)
Escalate to **BEACOPP**: 2-year relapse-free survival ~65%, against ~13% if ABVD continues
Salvage chemo then **high-dose (BEAM) autologous SCT**, ideally PET-negative first
Brentuximab vedotin, PD-1 inhibitors, allogeneic SCT
Early stage: RT alone; strongly CD20+, so rituximab-based therapy is an option

blocks.title: Regimens to decode
items: **ABVD**: doxorubicin (**A**driamycin), **b**leomycin, **v**inblastine, **d**acarbazine. It is non-sterilising and carries a low risk of second cancer.
**BEACOPP**: bleomycin, etoposide, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, vincristine (Oncovin), procarbazine, prednisolone. It is more toxic, with more late effects.
**BEAM** (autograft conditioning): carmustine (BCNU), etoposide, cytarabine, melphalan.

blocks.title: Targeted therapy in HL
items: **Brentuximab vedotin**: an antibody–drug conjugate against **CD30** on RS cells that delivers the antimitotic **monomethyl auristatin E**. It is used after failure of autograft or when the patient is unfit for one, and as a bridge to allograft. It can replace bleomycin in advanced disease, at the cost of more toxicity.
**PD-1 blockade** (pembrolizumab, nivolumab) gives useful responses in relapsed or refractory HL.

blocks.title: Late effects of HL treatment
items: **Breast cancer** after chest RT in young women, so they need a screening programme. **Lung cancer** in smokers after lung irradiation.
Cardiac disease from **doxorubicin** and RT; pulmonary toxicity from **bleomycin**.
**Hypothyroidism** after neck RT, so check TSH annually.
Second cancers overall (~4.6×, for decades), including leukaemia/MDS.
ABVD has a **low** risk of infertility and secondary MDS/AML.

blocks.text: **Omitting RT in early HL:** Kumar & Clark says RT should not be dropped because relapse rises slightly. Davidson (RAPID trial) says non-bulky patients who are **PET-negative after 3 ABVD can safely omit RT**. Follow Davidson.
Cycle numbers for advanced HL vary: the Essentials says 8 ABVD, Pocket Medicine 6 (PET-adapted). Davidson's answer is **6–8 cycles, guided by interim PET-2**.

sections.title: Management of non-Hodgkin lymphoma & targeted therapy

blocks.title: Low-grade (follicular) NHL
items: **80%** present at an advanced stage and follow a relapsing–remitting course over years.
**Watch and wait** if asymptomatic.
Treat for: marked systemic symptoms, uncomfortable or disfiguring nodes, **marrow failure**, or **compression** syndromes.
Localised stage I disease (rare): **radiotherapy**.
Chemo-immunotherapy: **R-CVP, R-CHOP or R-bendamustine**. Oral chlorambucil is well tolerated but not curative.
**Rituximab maintenance** for 2 years delays relapse but has not improved survival.
Relapse: idelalisib (PI3K inhibitor); high-dose chemotherapy with autologous SCT.

blocks.title: High-grade NHL (DLBCL)
items: Treat **at diagnosis**: untreated, it is fatal within months.
**R-CHOP** is first line for stage II and above, usually **6 cycles** in advanced disease.
Stage I non-bulky: 4 cycles of (R-)CHOP then involved-site RT. RT is also used for residual bulk and compression syndromes.
Cardiac impairment: **R-GCVP** (gemcitabine replaces doxorubicin).
**CNS prophylaxis** (intrathecal or high-dose methotrexate) for high CNS risk: raised LDH with > 2 extranodal sites, or testis, breast or epidural disease.
Chemo-sensitive relapse: salvage then **autologous HSCT**. Pocket Medicine also lists **CAR-T** cells for relapsed disease.

blocks.title: Other subtypes
rows: Urgent intensive regimen: high-dose cyclophosphamide, methotrexate and cytarabine (e.g. CODOX-M/IVAC, DA-EPOCH-R), with **mandatory CNS prophylaxis** and tumour-lysis prophylaxis. Curative intent regardless of HIV status.
**_H. pylori_ eradication**, with endoscopy and biopsy at 6, 12 and 24 months. If it persists: rituximab ± chemotherapy or low-dose RT.
Intensive chemo-immunotherapy ± autograft in the fit; **ibrutinib (BTK inhibitor)** at relapse
CHOP-type combination chemotherapy **without rituximab** (T cells lack CD20); worse outcomes
Give antiretroviral therapy alongside chemotherapy; avoid rituximab if **CD4 < 50**

blocks.title: Antibodies and targeted drugs
rows: Anti-**CD20**. Up to 60% durable responses alone, and synergy with chemo. Added to CHOP, it raises CR rates and overall survival.
Newer anti-CD20. With chemo it improves PFS in follicular lymphoma but is more toxic.
Anti-**CD30** drug conjugate: relapsed/refractory Hodgkin lymphoma; can replace bleomycin in advanced HL

blocks.text: **CHOP** = cyclophosphamide, **H**ydroxydaunorubicin (doxorubicin), **O**ncovin (vincristine), prednisolone. Check **echo** before the anthracycline and **HBsAg + anti-HBc** before rituximab, because rituximab can reactivate HBV.

Quoted DLBCL cure rates vary widely: Step-Up gives an older "85% with CHOP", the Essentials 60–70% cure in early stage with R-CHOP, and Davidson ~50% disease-free at 5 years overall. For exams, quote **Davidson** and remember that the IPI stratifies the figure.

cards.front: Lineage split of NHL (Davidson)?
Age distribution of Hodgkin lymphoma?
Which virus causes adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma?
Infection linked to ocular MALT lymphoma?
t(14;18) — which lymphoma, which gene?
t(11;14) — which lymphoma, which protein?
Immunophenotype of the classical Reed–Sternberg cell?
Commonest HL subtype and its typical patient?
cards.back: **Nodular sclerosing** (~70%): young adults, women, mediastinal disease.

cards.front: Two HL symptoms that do NOT count as B symptoms?
Marrow involvement: low-grade vs high-grade NHL?
Why is FNA inadequate to diagnose lymphoma?
cards.back: The **nodal architecture** is needed, so take an excision (or core) biopsy.

cards.front: Serology needed before rituximab?
cards.back: **HBsAg and anti-HBc** (HBV reactivation risk), plus HCV and HIV.

cards.front: Ann Arbor stage III?
cards.back: Node regions on **both sides of the diaphragm** (± spleen, S).

cards.front: Suffix X in Cotswolds staging?
cards.back: **Bulk**: mediastinal widening > 1/3 or nodal mass > 10 cm.

cards.front: The seven Hasenclever factors?
cards.back: Age > 45, male, albumin < 40 g/L, Hb < 105 g/L, stage IV, WCC > 15, lymphocytes < 0.6 (× 10⁹/L).

cards.front: Rate of transformation of low-grade NHL to high grade?
cards.back: ~**3% per year**, with poor survival afterwards.

cards.front: ABVD components?
Advanced HL still PET-positive after 2 ABVD — next?
Brentuximab vedotin — target and payload?
cards.back: Anti-**CD30** antibody delivering monomethyl auristatin E.

cards.front: First-line therapy for stage II+ DLBCL?
First-line therapy for localised low-grade gastric MALT lymphoma?

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman who grew up in the Caribbean presents with generalised lymphadenopathy and a skin rash. Biopsy shows a mature **T-cell** lymphoma, and abnormal lymphocytes are circulating in her blood.
questions.leadIn: Which infection is most likely to be causally linked to her lymphoma?
questions.explanation: A T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma in someone from an HTLV-1-endemic area (Caribbean, Japan) points to **adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma**, caused by **HTLV-1**.
whyNot: EBV is linked to Burkitt and post-transplant B-cell lymphomas, not adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma.
HHV-8 is linked to primary effusion lymphoma.
_H. pylori_ drives gastric MALT (B-cell) lymphoma.
Hepatitis C is a general NHL risk factor without this T-cell/geographic pattern.

questions.stem: A student is comparing the epidemiology of Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma using Davidson's figures.
questions.leadIn: Which feature is typical of non-Hodgkin lymphoma rather than Hodgkin lymphoma?
options: Median age at diagnosis of about 31 years
Bimodal age peaks at 20–35 and 50–70 years
Median age at diagnosis of 65–70 years
Higher rates in well-educated people from small families
Threefold higher risk after infectious mononucleosis
questions.explanation: NHL has a **median age of 65–70 years** and its incidence keeps rising with age. All the other features describe **Hodgkin lymphoma**.
whyNot: A median age of 31 describes HL.
The bimodal pattern belongs to HL.
This social-class association is described for HL.
The post-glandular-fever risk is described for HL.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman has a dry cough and a large anterior mediastinal mass. A supraclavicular node biopsy shows bands of collagen dividing the node into nodules. Scattered large binucleate cells are **CD15+ and CD30+**, set in a background of eosinophils, plasma cells and T cells.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The CD15+/CD30+ Reed–Sternberg cells mean **classical HL**. Collagen bands in a young woman with mediastinal disease mean **nodular sclerosis**, the commonest subtype (~70%).
whyNot: Mixed cellularity favours older patients and lacks collagen bands.
Lymphocyte-depleted HL is rare, seen with HIV and in older men, and shows few background lymphocytes.
NLPHL has CD20+ "popcorn" cells and is not CD15/CD30-type classical HL.
Follicular lymphoma is a low-grade B-cell NHL with no Reed–Sternberg cells.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man has generalised lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly and abnormal lymphocytes in his blood that were first thought to be CLL. Immunohistochemistry on a node biopsy shows strong nuclear **cyclin D1** expression.
questions.leadIn: Which chromosomal translocation is most likely present?
questions.explanation: Cyclin D1 overexpression from **t(11;14)** (CCND1–IGH) defines **mantle cell lymphoma**, which can mimic CLL in the blood.
whyNot: t(14;18) upregulates BCL2 in follicular lymphoma.
t(8;14) deregulates MYC in Burkitt lymphoma.
t(2;5) creates NPM1–ALK in anaplastic large-cell lymphoma.
t(11;18) occurs in MALT lymphoma.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old man has a 2-month history of a painless, rubbery left supraclavicular node. He has generalised itch and the node aches after he drinks beer. He has lost 3 kg (4% of his body weight) and denies fevers or night sweats. Biopsy confirms classical Hodgkin lymphoma.
questions.leadIn: Which statement about his symptoms and staging is correct?
options: His pruritus makes him category B
His alcohol-induced pain makes him category B
His weight loss makes him category B
He is category A because none of his symptoms are B symptoms
Supraclavicular involvement adds the suffix E
questions.explanation: B symptoms are only **fever > 38°C, drenching night sweats and > 10% weight loss in 6 months**. Itch and alcohol-induced pain are classic HL features but are **not counted**, and 4% weight loss is below the threshold, so he is **A**.
whyNot: Pruritus is a recognised HL symptom but is not a staging B symptom.
Alcohol-related nodal pain is a classic clue but does not count for staging.
Weight loss must exceed 10% within 6 months.
E denotes contiguous extranodal disease; a supraclavicular node is nodal.

questions.stem: You are teaching a student how the presentations of Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma differ.
questions.leadIn: Which finding at presentation favours NHL over HL?
options: A single cervical node with orderly spread to the next node group
Extranodal disease in the stomach and testis
Pain in the nodes after drinking alcohol
A large, surprisingly asymptomatic mediastinal mass in a young woman
questions.explanation: NHL is often **disseminated and extranodal** at diagnosis (gut, testis, thyroid, skin, marrow, brain). HL spreads contiguously and rarely goes extranodal.
whyNot: Contiguous node-to-node spread is typical of HL.
Alcohol-induced nodal pain is a classic HL clue.
This is typical of nodular sclerosing HL.
Fluctuating nodes are described in HL.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man has a 2.5 cm painless, rubbery cervical node that has persisted for 6 weeks. There are no signs of infection, and a CXR is normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate investigation to establish the diagnosis?
options: Fine needle aspiration cytology of the node
questions.explanation: Lymphoma needs a **tissue diagnosis with preserved architecture**, so excise the node for histology, immunophenotyping and molecular studies.
whyNot: FNA loses the nodal architecture and is inadequate for diagnosing lymphoma.
Marrow biopsy is for staging, not first diagnosis.
PET-CT stages disease and guides biopsy, but cannot give histology.
LDH is non-specific and prognostic only.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with newly diagnosed stage III diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is about to start R-CHOP.
questions.leadIn: Which blood test is essential before the first dose of rituximab?
options: Hepatitis B surface antigen and core antibody
questions.explanation: Rituximab can **reactivate hepatitis B**, so HBsAg and anti-HBc (plus HCV and HIV) must be checked before therapy.
whyNot: ACE is a sarcoidosis marker with no role before rituximab.
Free light chains are used in myeloma work-up.
ANA screens for connective tissue disease, not a rituximab safety check.
Ferritin has no role in pre-rituximab screening.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with classical Hodgkin lymphoma has involved cervical and mediastinal nodes. PET-CT also shows splenic involvement but no other extranodal disease. She reports drenching night sweats.
questions.leadIn: What is her Ann Arbor stage?
questions.explanation: Disease above the diaphragm plus the **spleen** (below it) = **stage III with S**. Night sweats add **B**.
whyNot: Stage II requires all disease on one side of the diaphragm; the spleen lies below it.
Her night sweats make her B, not A.
Stage IV needs diffuse extralymphatic disease (e.g. liver, marrow); the spleen is a lymphatic organ.
E denotes a contiguous extranodal site, and her disease spans both sides of the diaphragm.

questions.stem: A patient with advanced Hodgkin lymphoma is being scored on the Hasenclever index.
questions.leadIn: Which finding scores a point?
questions.explanation: Points are scored for albumin **< 40 g/L**, age > 45, male sex, Hb < 105 g/L, stage IV, WCC > 15 × 10⁹/L and lymphocytes < 0.6 × 10⁹/L.
whyNot: Age must exceed 45 years.
Male, not female, sex scores.
Hb must be below 105 g/L.
WCC must exceed 15 × 10⁹/L.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman has stage IIA classical Hodgkin lymphoma confined to the neck. There is no bulky disease and her ESR is normal.
questions.leadIn: According to Davidson, what is the standard treatment?
options: Two cycles of ABVD followed by 20 Gy involved-site radiotherapy
questions.explanation: Early-stage HL **without risk factors** gets **2 × ABVD + 20 Gy** involved-site RT. Combined therapy beats RT alone.
whyNot: Trials show combined chemo-RT outperforms RT alone in early-stage HL.
BEACOPP is reserved for advanced disease that is PET-positive after 2 ABVD.
R-CHOP is for DLBCL, not classical HL.
Classical HL is treated with curative intent at diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with stage IVB Hodgkin lymphoma has had two cycles of ABVD. An interim PET-CT still shows intense FDG uptake in several nodal sites.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Continue ABVD for four more cycles
Omit bleomycin and continue with AVD
questions.explanation: A **positive PET-2** predicts a very high relapse risk on ABVD (only ~13% relapse-free at 2 years). Escalating to **BEACOPP** raises relapse-free survival to about 65%.
whyNot: Continuing ABVD after a positive PET-2 gives poor results.
Dropping bleomycin is for PET-negative patients.
Active advanced disease must be treated.
RT alone is not curative for advanced-stage HL.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man is found to have stage IIIA follicular lymphoma. He feels well. His blood count is normal, and there is no organ compression or bulky disease.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation: Low-grade NHL is **not curable** with conventional therapy, and a well patient (no symptoms, organ impairment, bulk or rapid progression) is managed expectantly. Use **watch and wait** until symptoms, cytopenias or compression develop.
whyNot: Chemo-immunotherapy is held until there is a treatment indication.
Autologous SCT is reserved for relapsed disease.
RT is used for rare localised stage I disease.
Ibrutinib is for relapsed mantle cell lymphoma.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman has dyspepsia. Endoscopic biopsy shows a low-grade marginal zone B-cell lymphoma confined to the stomach, and a urease test is positive.
questions.leadIn: What is the treatment of choice?
questions.explanation: Localised low-grade **gastric MALT** lymphoma often regresses with **_H. pylori_ eradication** alone, with endoscopic re-evaluation at 6, 12 and 24 months.
whyNot: Surgery is rarely needed.
Chemo-immunotherapy is for persistent or transformed disease.
Low-dose RT is used if the lymphoma persists after eradication.
Brentuximab targets CD30 and is used mainly in HL.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the best option from the list above. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 7-year-old boy from rural Uganda has a mass in his mandible that has grown visibly over 3 weeks. Biopsy shows a very high proliferation fraction, and the MYC gene is rearranged.
items.explanation: A rapidly growing **jaw tumour** in an equatorial African child with **MYC** rearrangement is **endemic Burkitt lymphoma** (EBV-associated).

items.stem: A 61-year-old woman has had slowly enlarging painless nodes at several sites for 4 years. Node histology shows a nodular pattern, and the cells overexpress an anti-apoptotic protein because of t(14;18).
items.explanation: An indolent course, a **nodular** pattern and **t(14;18)/BCL2** mean **follicular lymphoma**.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man with dyspepsia has a low-grade marginal-zone B-cell infiltrate in a gastric biopsy, and the rapid urease test is positive.
items.explanation: A low-grade gastric lymphoma with _H. pylori_ infection is **gastric MALT lymphoma**.

items.stem: A 57-year-old man has had itchy, eczema-like patches for years that have now spread to cover almost all his skin. Skin biopsy shows infiltrating atypical T cells, and the blood film is normal.
items.explanation: Eczematoid lesions progressing to erythroderma from a skin-based **T-cell** lymphoma, without blood involvement, is **mycosis fungoides** (Sézary syndrome adds circulating cells).

items.stem: A 38-year-old man with advanced HIV develops a large pleural effusion. Cytology shows malignant lymphoid cells infected with human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8). Imaging shows no solid mass.
items.explanation: **HHV-8** is the virus linked with **primary effusion lymphoma**, which fits a malignant lymphomatous effusion with no solid mass.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man has sporadic Burkitt lymphoma with bulky abdominal disease. Before chemotherapy his serum urate is very high and his creatinine is at the upper limit of normal.
questions.leadIn: Which measure is most important as treatment starts?
options: Rasburicase prophylaxis with very frequent potassium and phosphate monitoring for at least 72 hours
Start allopurinol only after the first cycle has finished
Delay chemotherapy for 4 weeks until the urate normalises
Oral potassium supplements to prevent hypokalaemia
Fluid restriction to reduce tumour oedema
questions.explanation: Burkitt is the fastest-growing lymphoma, and its cells break down rapidly on treatment (**tumour lysis**). Give **rasburicase** and check potassium and phosphate very frequently for ≥ 72 h.
whyNot: Prophylaxis must start before cytotoxic therapy, not after.
Burkitt progresses too quickly to delay treatment.
Tumour lysis causes hyperkalaemia, so potassium supplements are dangerous.
Fluid restriction worsens urate nephropathy; hydration is needed.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man with stage IV diffuse large B-cell lymphoma has severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction on echocardiography.
questions.leadIn: Which regimen is preferred?
questions.explanation: In cardiac impairment, **R-GCVP** replaces the anthracycline doxorubicin with **gemcitabine**.
whyNot: The doxorubicin in CHOP is cardiotoxic.
ABVD is an HL regimen and also contains doxorubicin.
Chlorambucil is a palliative oral drug for low-grade disease.
BEACOPP is an intensive HL regimen with an anthracycline.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman was treated at 19 for Hodgkin lymphoma with chemotherapy and mediastinal radiotherapy. She is now well and in long-term follow-up.
questions.leadIn: Which surveillance is most specifically indicated by her treatment history?
options: Entry to a breast cancer screening programme
Annual stool for occult blood from age 25
questions.explanation: Young women given **chest irradiation** have a raised **breast cancer** risk and should take part in screening. Neck RT also warrants annual TSH.
whyNot: PSA is irrelevant in a woman.
Routine marrow biopsy is not used for surveillance.
There is no specific gastric risk from mediastinal RT.
Colorectal screening is not specifically indicated by HL treatment.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man has stage II diffuse large B-cell lymphoma with one extranodal site. His LDH is normal and he is fully active (ECOG 0).
questions.leadIn: Which new finding would move him into a higher IPI risk group?
options: Serum LDH above the upper limit of normal
Involvement of cervical rather than axillary nodes
questions.explanation: The IPI scores **age > 60, stage III–IV, > 1 extranodal site, raised LDH and poor performance status**. A raised LDH would add a point.
whyNot: Lineage is not an IPI factor.
The specific node group is not scored.
Normal Hb is not an IPI factor (Hb is in FLIPI, and there it counts when < 120 g/L).
B symptoms are not in the IPI.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man has stage IVB classical Hodgkin lymphoma. Results: albumin 36 g/L, Hb 110 g/L, WCC 12 × 10⁹/L, lymphocytes 0.8 × 10⁹/L.
questions.leadIn: What is his Hasenclever score?
questions.explanation: Work through all seven factors in turn. **Age > 45:** yes (1). **Male:** yes (2). **Albumin < 40 g/L:** 36, yes (3). **Hb < 105 g/L:** 110, no. **Stage IV:** yes (4). **WCC > 15:** 12, no. **Lymphocytes < 0.6:** 0.8, no. The total is **4**. The trap is scoring the "nearly abnormal" Hb and lymphocyte values; each cut-off is strict.
whyNot: This misses at least two of age, sex, albumin and stage.
This misses one positive factor, usually albumin or stage IV.
This wrongly scores Hb 110 or lymphocytes 0.8, neither of which crosses its threshold.
This wrongly scores both borderline values.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old woman has a 6-week dry cough and mild breathlessness. CXR shows an anterior mediastinal mass. On examination she has a 3 cm rubbery right supraclavicular node.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step to make the diagnosis?
options: Excision biopsy of the supraclavicular node
Fine needle aspiration of the supraclavicular node
questions.explanation: Step 1: a young woman with a mediastinal mass, cough and a rubbery node suggests **nodular sclerosing HL** (or another lymphoma). Step 2: lymphoma needs **architecture-preserving histology**. Step 3: choose the most accessible involved tissue, the **supraclavicular node**, rather than a mediastinal procedure. Excise it for histology, immunophenotyping and molecular work.
whyNot: FNA cannot assess nodal architecture.
Steroids can shrink lymphoma and spoil the histology; treatment comes after diagnosis.
Sputum cytology does not sample a nodal mass.
Marrow biopsy stages disease but rarely makes the first diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man with HIV, not on treatment, has a CD4 count of 30 cells/µL. He is diagnosed with advanced diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.
questions.leadIn: Which treatment approach is most appropriate?
options: CHOP-based chemotherapy with concurrent antiretroviral therapy, omitting rituximab
Watch and wait until the CD4 count recovers
questions.explanation: Step 1: HIV-related NHL is treated with curative intent, much like disease in HIV-negative patients. Step 2: **giving antiretroviral therapy alongside chemotherapy** improves survival. Step 3: with **CD4 < 50**, rituximab raises the risk of death from infection, so leave it out. The answer is CHOP-based chemotherapy with concurrent antiretroviral therapy.
whyNot: Stopping antiretrovirals removes their survival benefit, and rituximab is risky at CD4 < 50.
DLBCL is rapidly fatal if untreated.
Single-agent rituximab is inadequate for DLBCL and risky at this CD4 count.
RT alone does not treat advanced disease.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the best option from the list above. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Two cycles of ABVD + 20 Gy involved-site radiotherapy
Four cycles of ABVD + 30 Gy involved-site radiotherapy
Salvage chemotherapy then high-dose autologous stem cell transplant
Intensive high-dose cyclophosphamide/methotrexate/cytarabine with CNS prophylaxis

items.stem: A 73-year-old woman has asymptomatic stage IIIA follicular lymphoma with normal blood counts and no compressive disease.
items.explanation: Asymptomatic advanced low-grade NHL: **watch and wait**.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man has stage IIA classical Hodgkin lymphoma with an 11 cm mediastinal mass.
items.explanation: Two steps: a mass > 10 cm is **bulk**, a risk factor, so early-stage disease gets **4 × ABVD + 30 Gy**.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman relapses with Hodgkin lymphoma 18 months after completing ABVD. She is fit.
items.explanation: Relapsed HL is treated with **salvage chemotherapy** aiming for PET-negative remission, then a **BEAM autograft**.

items.stem: A 67-year-old man with mantle cell lymphoma relapses after chemo-immunotherapy.
items.explanation: The **BTK inhibitor ibrutinib** is approved for relapsed mantle cell lymphoma.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man has stage IV peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified.
items.explanation: T cells do not express **CD20**, so treat with DLBCL-type combination chemotherapy **without rituximab**.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man has newly diagnosed classical Hodgkin lymphoma, and his baseline full blood count is reviewed.
questions.leadIn: Which finding is a poor prognostic factor?
questions.explanation: In HL, a **normocytic anaemia or lymphopenia** carries a worse prognosis. Lymphopenia < 0.6 × 10⁹/L is also a Hasenclever factor.
whyNot: Eosinophilia may occur in HL but is not listed as adverse.
Neutrophilia may be seen but is not a listed adverse factor.
A normal Hb is not adverse; anaemia is.
A normal platelet count carries no adverse weight.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man has stage IV diffuse large B-cell lymphoma involving the testis. His LDH is raised.
questions.leadIn: In addition to R-CHOP, what should he receive?
options: Intrathecal or high-dose methotrexate as CNS prophylaxis
questions.explanation: Testicular, breast or epidural disease, or a high LDH with > 2 extranodal sites, carries a **high CNS relapse risk**. Give **intrathecal or high-dose methotrexate**.
whyNot: Cranial RT is not the recommended prophylaxis here.
Brentuximab targets CD30 and has no role in standard DLBCL CNS prophylaxis.
Rituximab maintenance is not CNS prophylaxis; the CNS-directed options are intrathecal methotrexate or high-dose methotrexate, which crosses the blood–brain barrier.
Testicular involvement is a recognised indication for CNS prophylaxis.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman has a thyroid mass from diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, with involved nodes in the adjacent neck. There is no disease below the diaphragm.
questions.leadIn: What is her Ann Arbor stage?
questions.explanation: An **extralymphatic site plus lymph node regions on the same side** of the diaphragm is **IIE**.
whyNot: Stage I covers a single node region only.
IE is a single extralymphatic site without node involvement.
Stage III needs disease on both sides of the diaphragm.
Stage IV means diffuse extralymphatic disease, not one localised contiguous site.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man with classical Hodgkin lymphoma relapses after an autologous stem cell transplant. His team plans an antibody–drug conjugate.
questions.leadIn: Which antigen does this drug target?
questions.explanation: **Brentuximab vedotin** binds **CD30** on Reed–Sternberg cells and releases monomethyl auristatin E inside them.
whyNot: CD20 is the rituximab target; classical RS cells are usually CD20-negative.
CD19 is a B-cell antigen, but it is not the target of brentuximab vedotin.
CD15 is a diagnostic marker of RS cells but not a drug target.
PD-1 is blocked by pembrolizumab or nivolumab, which are antibodies, not drug conjugates.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man has had follicular lymphoma on watch and wait for 6 years. Over 3 weeks one abdominal node has grown rapidly. He has night sweats, and his LDH has risen sharply.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Repeat the blood count in 3 months
questions.explanation: Step 1: sudden growth, B symptoms and a rising LDH in follicular lymphoma suggest **transformation to DLBCL** (~3% per year). Step 2: transformation is proven histologically, so **re-biopsy** before choosing aggressive treatment.
whyNot: This picture needs urgent assessment, not less follow-up.
Maintenance does not treat a transformed high-grade lymphoma.
This is not gastric MALT lymphoma.
Waiting risks progression of a high-grade lymphoma.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman asks whether anything in her past increases her risk of Hodgkin lymphoma.
questions.leadIn: Which history is most clearly associated with a higher risk of Hodgkin lymphoma?
questions.explanation: A past history of **infectious mononucleosis** makes HL about **three times** more likely, though EBV has not been proven causal.
whyNot: _H. pylori_ is linked with gastric MALT lymphoma.
HTLV-1 causes adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma.
Hepatitis C is a risk factor for NHL.
_C. psittaci_ is linked with ocular MALT lymphoma.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl from Malawi has a rapidly enlarging tumour of the jaw. Biopsy shows sheets of medium-sized B cells with a very high proliferation rate, and the tumour is EBV-positive.
questions.leadIn: Which cytogenetic abnormality is most likely?
questions.explanation: This is **endemic Burkitt lymphoma**, defined by **t(8;14)**, which moves MYC next to the IGH locus.
whyNot: t(14;18) is the follicular lymphoma translocation.
t(11;14) is typical of mantle cell lymphoma.
t(2;5) is typical of anaplastic large-cell lymphoma.
t(11;18) occurs in MALT lymphoma.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man is on his fourth cycle of ABVD for Hodgkin lymphoma. He develops a dry cough and exertional breathlessness, and lung function shows a reduced transfer factor.
questions.leadIn: Which drug is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: **Bleomycin** causes the pulmonary toxicity of ABVD, which is why it is dropped (AVD) when interim PET is negative.
whyNot: Doxorubicin causes cardiac toxicity.
Vinblastine is not the recognised cause of ABVD lung toxicity.
Dacarbazine is not the lung-toxic component.
Procarbazine is part of BEACOPP, not ABVD.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man has a single enlarged cervical node. Biopsy shows a nodular infiltrate with scattered large "popcorn" cells that are strongly **CD20-positive** and negative for CD15 and CD30.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: CD20+ **popcorn** cells without the classical CD15/CD30 profile define **NLPHL**, a non-classical HL that behaves like low-grade B-cell NHL.
whyNot: Classical subtypes have CD15+/CD30+ RS cells.
Classical subtypes have CD15+/CD30+ RS cells.
Lymphocyte-rich HL is a classical subtype with CD15+/CD30+ cells.
Burkitt is a high-grade lymphoma of monotonous medium-sized cells, not popcorn cells.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman finishes six cycles of ABVD for advanced Hodgkin lymphoma. CT shows a 4 cm residual mediastinal mass, but PET shows **no FDG uptake** in it.
questions.leadIn: What does this finding most likely represent?
options: Inactive fibrotic or necrotic residue consistent with complete metabolic response
Active lymphoma needing escalation to BEACOPP
questions.explanation: PET separates **active tumour (avid)** from **fibrosis or necrosis (non-avid)**. A PET-negative residual mass is a complete metabolic response, and radiotherapy can often be omitted.
whyNot: Escalation is for FDG-avid (PET-positive) disease.
Nothing suggests a new high-grade process, and the mass is metabolically inactive.
There are no features of infection, and active TB would usually be FDG-avid.
She has had no radiotherapy and is just finishing treatment.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with long-standing Sjögren syndrome develops a progressively enlarging, painless parotid swelling. Biopsy shows a low-grade B-cell infiltrate arising in mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Chronic autoimmune inflammation of the salivary glands (Sjögren) predisposes to **MALT lymphoma** of the salivary gland.
whyNot: Burkitt is high-grade, with jaw or abdominal masses in the young.
HL presents with nodal disease and Reed–Sternberg cells.
Mantle cell lymphoma presents with generalised nodes, marrow and blood involvement in older men.
Mycosis fungoides is a cutaneous T-cell lymphoma.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man with newly diagnosed classical Hodgkin lymphoma has a baseline PET-CT for staging.
questions.leadIn: Which staging investigation can usually be omitted when PET-CT is used?
questions.explanation: PET-CT assesses marrow involvement well enough that **marrow biopsy is needed only if PET is not used** for marrow staging.
whyNot: FBC is part of every lymphoma work-up and has prognostic value.
LDH is an adverse prognostic marker and is always checked.
HIV status affects treatment decisions and is routinely tested.
Cardiac function is checked before anthracycline-containing chemotherapy.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old man with HIV and a CD4 count of 25 cells/µL develops headache and confusion. MRI shows an enhancing periventricular mass. Brain biopsy shows a diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, and EBV is detected in the tumour.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: This is **primary CNS lymphoma** (very low CD4, EBV-driven). It is treated with a **high-dose methotrexate**-based regimen, which crosses the blood–brain barrier, plus steroids ± RT.
whyNot: ABVD is a Hodgkin regimen.
CHOP drugs penetrate the CNS poorly.
PCNSL is rapidly fatal if untreated.
The biopsy has already shown lymphoma rather than toxoplasmosis.

ospe.identify: **Reed–Sternberg cell**: large binucleate cell with prominent eosinophilic nucleoli ("owl's eyes") among reactive small lymphocytes. Diagnosis: **Hodgkin lymphoma**.
Classical HL histology: scattered mononuclear Hodgkin cells and a binucleate Reed–Sternberg cell in a background of benign lymphocytes and histiocytes.
NHL architecture: a **follicular/nodular** pattern means **low grade**, and diffuse effacement means **high grade**.
CXR: **mediastinal mass** (widened mediastinum) from Hodgkin lymphoma. Think of a young woman with nodular sclerosing HL and cough.
Anterior mediastinal mass deviating the trachea. PET-CT is **FDG-avid** at diagnosis and **PET-negative** (complete metabolic response) after treatment.
**Bulky axillary lymphadenopathy** with distended superficial veins: high-grade NHL.
Child with jaw/facial swelling: **endemic Burkitt lymphoma** (EBV, malaria belt, t(8;14)).
Blood film of **mantle cell lymphoma** cells that can mimic CLL. Confirm by immunophenotyping/cytogenetics (t(11;14), cyclin D1).
